analysis.one_liner: Gives Medicare beneficiaries a drug discount card and caps yearly out-of-pocket drug costs.
analysis.headline: Introduced July 25, 2001 with three Republican cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day and never received a vote or further action before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a voluntary Medicare prescription drug program. Seniors could enroll for a $25 annual fee (waived for lower incomes) and get a card giving them access to negotiated drug discounts, plus a catastrophic backstop that stops their yearly out-of-pocket drug costs at $1,200 for the lowest-income seniors, $2,500 for middle incomes, and $5,000 for others. Private companies—pharmacy benefit managers, insurers, pharmacies, and Medicare HMOs—would compete on bids to administer the benefit, and the government would pick up the costs the $25 fees don't cover, from Medicare's trust fund.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who pay for their own prescriptions, especially lower-income seniors facing high drug bills. The catastrophic protection means their annual out-of-pocket drug spending stops at a fixed ceiling, and the $25 enrollment fee is waived for anyone under 200% of the poverty line. Independent pharmacies would gain, too, since contractors must let any local pharmacy join their network.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors paying out of pocket for drugs

how_it_helps.text: Every enrollee gets access to negotiated prices and discounts on prescription drugs through a standard card, including in areas where no contractor wins a bid.

A catastrophic benefit caps annual out-of-pocket drug costs at $1,200 for seniors under 200% of the poverty line, $2,500 for those between 200% and 400%, and $5,000 above that—and the government, not the contractor, bears that risk.
The $25 annual enrollment fee is waived for seniors with incomes below 200% of the poverty line.

Enrollee protections include guaranteed issue regardless of health status, formulary rules requiring coverage across all drug categories, appeals for denied drugs, a right for any area pharmacy to join a contractor's network, and a medication therapy management program to reduce dangerous drug interactions.
Costs beyond the enrollment fees are paid from Medicare's Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund, with general Treasury appropriations to cover the shortfall.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, through Medicare's trust fund and general appropriations, cover the catastrophic benefit and whatever the $25 enrollment fees don't pay for. Drug makers would face negotiated discounts from the private contractors. Medigap insurers would lose the drug-coverage portion of their most comprehensive policies, which the bill requires to be redesigned so they complement rather than duplicate the new benefit. A new independent Medicare Prescription Drug Agency would be created and staffed at public expense.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers; drug makers face negotiated discounts

drawbacks.text: The protection is thin at the front end: enrollees get only access to negotiated prices, with no guaranteed discount amount and no defined drug coverage, and even under the catastrophic backstop a low-income senior pays the first $1,200 a year and a higher-income senior pays the first $5,000.

The benefit is delivered through private pharmacy benefit managers and insurers, who receive a negotiated administrative fee for every prescription filled under the catastrophic benefit—adding a middleman layer whose costs the bill leaves to be set 'consistent with fees paid under private sector pharmaceutical benefit contracts.'
Seniors above 600% of the poverty line get the discount card but no catastrophic protection at all.

The bill creates a new independent executive agency with a Senate-confirmed Commissioner serving a six-year term, a significant government reorganization for a program that is voluntary and discount-based rather than a full drug benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For seniors with high drug bills, the catastrophic caps are real, immediate relief and the government bears that risk directly, which is a stronger design than a pure private discount card. But the day-to-day benefit is modest—negotiated prices with no floor on how big the discount must be—and a permanent middleman layer of pharmacy benefit managers and insurers sits between the public money and the patient. It was also far short of the full Medicare drug benefit many advocates for seniors were pressing for at the time.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never reported it or brought it up, and it died there when the 107th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Chuck Hagel introduced the Medicare Rx Drug Discount and Security Act of 2001 on July 25, 2001, joined by original cosponsors Sen. John Ensign and Sen. Richard Lugar.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, where it was never taken up again.
The bill drew three Republican cosponsors and no Democratic support in the Senate.
No further action of any kind was recorded before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, so the bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or consideration by the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private drug-benefit intermediaries—pharmacy benefit managers, insurers, and drug makers—kept the status quo, with no Medicare-contracted competition or negotiated discounts imposed on them. Medicare seniors went on paying full drug prices for the rest of the Congress with no federal benefit in place.

for.name: Chuck Hagel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and laid out the discount-card and catastrophic benefit design.

for.name: 3 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. John Ensign and Richard Lugar.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral in the 107th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out, held no markup, and never brought it to the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: Only Republicans backed the bill—3 of 49 Senate Republican cosponsors and no Democrats—so it never attracted bipartisan sponsorship, and with no vote ever taken, the parties' positions on the merits were never measured.

industries.note: The bill names PBMs as eligible contractors and pays them an administrative fee on every prescription filled under the catastrophic benefit, making them the permanent channel for a public drug benefit. In exchange, they must compete on bids and disclose formulary, network, and appeal information, so seniors would gain discounts through them.

Insurers and Medicare+Choice plans could bid to become contractors and collect fees, but they must accept guaranteed issue, network and formulary rules, and appeal rights. Medigap insurers specifically lose the drug-coverage component of their top-tier policies, which the bill requires be redesigned to avoid duplicating the new benefit.

Contractors must let any pharmacy in a covered area join their network if it accepts the terms, protecting independent pharmacies from exclusion, and pharmacies are paid fees for running the medication therapy management program.

Drug makers would face negotiated discounts from private contractors serving millions of Medicare enrollees, but the bill sets no government price list and lets manufacturers' discounts be decided in private negotiations, so their pricing power largely survives.
